author: Carlos Martinez
title: Grip pressure and hand position on a direct drive wheel
description: Why a death grip hides force feedback detail in iRacing, how to hold a direct drive wheel, and a practice routine to test your own grip pressure.

sections.p: Midway through a long practice run, I noticed my forearms were tired and the car felt numb. I had changed nothing in the settings. The only difference was that I had been driving tense, gripping the rim as if the wheel might leave. On a MOZA R9 with a peak of ~9 N·m, that tension matters more than most people expect. A direct drive wheel sends fine information through the rim: the load building in a front tyre, the moment the rear goes light. A hand squeezing hard becomes a filter between that signal and your fingertips. This post covers how I hold the wheel, what the thumbs, shoulders and wrist are doing, and a short routine to check your own grip.

sections.h2: Why a death grip hides detail

sections.p: Your hands read force through small movements and pressure changes in the fingers and palm. When the muscles of the hand and forearm are fully contracted, that tissue is stiff, and a small change in torque no longer moves your fingers against the rim in a way you can sense. The detail was present at the wheelbase and never registers in your hands. Stiff arms also work as a brace. The wheel pushes, your arms push back, and part of the texture of the force is absorbed by muscle before it arrives as a clear signal.

Loud effects survive a tight grip. Kerb strikes and big bumps still come through, so the wheel feels alive and you assume nothing is missing. What disappears are the quiet cues: the slight lightening as the front starts to push wide, the gradual load build through a long corner, the small change when the rear begins to rotate. Those are the cues that tell you what the car will do next, and they are the ones a clenched hand cannot feel. If you want a fuller picture of what each part of the signal represents, iRacing force feedback explained walks through it.

A tight grip also makes your own inputs coarse. Corrections come from the shoulders and whole arms instead of the fingers and wrists, so a small slide gets a large correction. The large correction then feels like the wheel is fighting you, and the natural reaction is to grip harder. The loop feeds itself until the stint ends or the forearms give up.

For most cars I sit with my hands at roughly 9 and 3, symmetrical on the rim, with my elbows bent and hanging relaxed. The fingers wrap around the rim and the palm makes light contact. The target is a grip firm enough that the wheel could not be pulled out of my hands, and no firmer. Under cornering load the pressure rises a little on its own, and I let it. On a straight it should drop to something close to resting weight.

In cars with a lot of steering lock, I shuffle the wheel through slow corners and hairpins instead of crossing my arms. A direct drive base can return the wheel quickly after a spin or a snap of oversteer, and a crossed arm has nowhere to go. In formula cars with a small steering range, the hands barely move from 9 and 3 at all.

I keep my thumbs resting along the outside of the rim or on its front face. I do not hook them around the inside of a spoke or tuck them behind the rim. A sudden kickback from a wall hit or a snapping slide can whip a spoke into a hooked thumb, and a strong wheelbase can do real damage to a thumb that is in the wrong place. Thumbs on the outside also stay loose, which helps the fingers stay sensitive. Treat this as a habit that reduces the chance of injury, not as a guarantee against it.

During a spin I keep a light hold and let the wheel move with the force. I do not fight it and I do not let go entirely, because a wheel that spins freely at ~9 N·m class torque is something I want to guide instead of chase.

Tension travels. If the shoulders creep up toward the ears, the upper arms tighten, then the forearms, then the hands. I check my shoulders at the end of every straight and drop them. My back stays against the seat so the seat, and not the wheel, holds my body in place under braking and cornering.

Seat distance sets the rest. With my wrists resting on top of the rim at 12 o'clock, my arms should have a slight bend and my shoulders should stay in contact with the seat. Too far away and the arms stretch and lock. Too close and the elbows cramp against the ribs, which also causes tension. The wrists should stay close to neutral, with the forearm in line with the hand. A wrist bent sharply backward or sideways tires quickly and dulls feel, because the tendons are already near their limit before any force arrives.

Pedals connect to this. The MOZA CRP2 is a load cell pedal set, so braking is a matter of pressure, and hard pressure on the brake pedal often brings a clenched grip with it. I brace with my back and my left foot on the dead pedal, which leaves my arms free. My fixed aluminium cockpit does not flex, so the wheelbase force goes directly into my hands and body. That rigidity is useful, but it means any tension I add is also transmitted without loss, so relaxed arms matter more than they would on a flexible rig.

sections.h2: A practice routine to test your grip

sections.p: Do this in one session with every force feedback setting left alone. If you change the settings in the middle, you will not know whether grip or strength produced the difference.

olist: Choose a car you know well and a track with a mix of slow, medium and fast corners. Warm up for a few laps with your usual grip.
Run a baseline stint. Pay attention to where in a long corner you feel the front load build, and where you feel it ease. Write down two or three places on the track.
Squeeze deliberately for a couple of laps, as hard as you can sustain. Check whether those cues at your marked places are still there.
Relax on purpose. On straights, loosen until the wheel would move if you let go, then close the fingers just enough to hold it. Use this lighter grip through the same corners.

Rate your effort on a simple personal scale from 1 to 10 on the straights. Most people who try this find their normal grip sits higher than they believed, and the target is a comfortable low number on straights with a small rise in corners.
Provoke a gentle understeer in a safe, familiar corner by entering a little too fast. See whether you feel the wheel go light before the car runs wide, and whether the relaxed grip shows it sooner.
Repeat the whole test a few days later. Also note how your hands and forearms feel after a long stint, since fatigue is part of the result.

sections.tip: At the end of each straight, open your fingers for a moment and then close them again before turn-in. If you cannot do it without the car wobbling, the grip was too tight to begin with. Fixing it takes a few sessions, because the habit is mostly unconscious.

sections.h2: Check your grip before changing settings

sections.p: A numb wheel sends many drivers to the strength slider. Raising it can add effort that your hands then meet with more tension, which hides the detail again, and it can push peaks into clipping. Before changing anything, repeat the routine above. If the detail returns with a lighter grip, the settings may already be fine.

If you still want a baseline to compare against, the MOZA R9 iRacing settings post covers what I run and why. If the wheel feels heavy or sticky even with relaxed hands, look at damping and friction settings, since extra resistance makes you grip harder to control it. And if the strong moments feel flat instead of detailed, diagnosing clipping is the next step. Change one thing at a time and give each change a full stint before judging it.

faqs.q: How tight should I hold a direct drive wheel?
faqs.a: Hold it firmly enough that it could not be pulled out of your hands, and no firmer. On straights the grip should drop to something close to resting weight. Under cornering load it rises a little on its own. If your forearms ache after a short stint, the grip is probably too tight.

faqs.q: Does a tight grip really change what I feel in iRacing?
faqs.a: Yes. Stiff hand and forearm muscles reduce how well small torque changes reach your fingers. Large effects like kerbs still come through, but quiet cues such as the front going light or the rear starting to rotate become harder to notice.

faqs.q: Where should my thumbs go on the wheel?
faqs.a: Rest them along the outside of the rim or on its front face. Avoid hooking them around the inside of a spoke, because a sudden kickback from a collision or a snap of oversteer can whip the wheel into them. This lowers the chance of injury but does not remove it.

faqs.q: Should I turn up force strength if the wheel feels dull?
faqs.a: Test your grip first. A tense grip can make a wheel feel dull at any strength, and higher strength can lead to clipping. If the detail comes back with a lighter hold, leave the strength alone and change settings one at a time afterward.
